common_name: La Reine Rose (Antique Deep Pink Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown own-root shrubs in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: La Reine was raised by Jean Laffay in France and introduced around 1842, placing it among the very first roses classed as Hybrid Perpetual. Its large, globular, deep rose-pink flowers open densely double and quartered, carrying a strong, classic old-rose fragrance on an upright, vigorous shrub. It produces a heavy spring flush followed by scattered repeat bloom later in the season, especially with regular feeding and deadheading. Give it fertile, well-drained soil and prune moderately in late winter to remove old or crossing wood and encourage strong new canes.

common_name: Baroness Rothschild Rose (Antique Pale Pink Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown own-root shrubs in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Baroness Rothschild was introduced in France in 1868 by the breeder Jean Pernet (Pernet pere) and quickly became prized for its very large, cupped, pale pink blooms arranged in neat, symmetrical rows of petals. Unlike most Hybrid Perpetuals of its era, it carries only light fragrance, but its smooth, nearly thornless canes and refined bloom form made it a favorite exhibition rose in Victorian gardens. It flowers heavily in spring with modest repeat later in the season on a sturdy, upright shrub. Plant in full sun with fertile, well-drained soil and prune moderately in late winter to maintain vigor.

common_name: Victor Verdier Rose (Antique Cerise-Pink Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown own-root shrubs in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Victor Verdier was raised by Lacharme in France and introduced in 1859, and is historically significant as a Hybrid Perpetual whose brighter, cleaner coloring and refined form led some rose historians to call it the first Hybrid Tea. Its bright rose-pink to cerise blooms are large, full, and moderately fragrant, opening on an upright, vigorous shrub with a strong spring display and some later repeat. It performs best in fertile, well-drained soil with full sun and benefits from moderate pruning in late winter to keep growth productive. Deadhead spent blooms through the season to encourage further flowering.

common_name: Marie Baumann Rose (Antique Carmine-Crimson Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown own-root shrubs in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Marie Baumann is a nineteenth-century Hybrid Perpetual bred by the Baumann brothers of Bollwiller, Alsace, and introduced in France in 1863, valued in its day as a reliable exhibition rose for its richly colored, carmine-crimson blooms held in a classic high-centered, very double form. The flowers carry a strong, rich fragrance and appear in a strong spring flush with some later repeat on a sturdy, moderately upright shrub. It prefers full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, with moderate pruning in late winter to remove old wood and encourage new flowering canes. Regular deadheading helps extend its bloom season.

common_name: Prince Camille de Rohan Rose (Antique Dark Velvet Crimson Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown own-root shrubs in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade.

directions: Prince Camille de Rohan was raised by Eugene Verdier in France and introduced in 1861, and remains known among old rose growers as one of the darkest Hybrid Perpetuals, with velvety crimson-maroon petals that deepen toward a near-black edge as they age. The intensely fragrant blooms open from shapely buds on a moderately compact, somewhat lower-growing shrub compared to many of its class. Afternoon shade in hot climates helps protect the dark petals from sun scorch and preserves color depth. Prune moderately in late winter and feed regularly to support its strong spring flush and modest repeat bloom.

common_name: John Hopper Rose (Antique Rosy Crimson Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown own-root shrubs in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: John Hopper was raised by the English breeder Ward and introduced in 1862, becoming one of the more free-flowering Hybrid Perpetuals of its generation. Its bright rose blooms, shaded lilac with a deeper carmine center, open in loose, full form and are produced with better repeat through summer than many classmates. The vigorous, upright shrub performs reliably in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and responds well to moderate feeding. Prune in late winter to remove old canes and shape the plant, and deadhead through the season to sustain its flowering.

common_name: Ulrich Brunner Fils Rose (Antique Cherry-Red Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown own-root shrubs in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing room for tall growth.

directions: Ulrich Brunner Fils was raised by Antoine Levet pere in France and introduced in 1881, and grew into one of the tallest and most vigorous of the Hybrid Perpetuals still grown by heirloom rose enthusiasts. Its large, loosely double, brilliant cherry-red blooms open quickly and carry a moderate fragrance on long, sturdy stems well suited to cutting. The shrub can reach considerable height, so give it plenty of room or train it as a short climber against a support. Prune only lightly in late winter, since hard pruning tends to reduce its naturally tall, arching habit and overall bloom production.

common_name: Eugene Furst Rose (Antique Deep Red Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown own-root shrubs in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Eugene Furst was introduced by the Luxembourg nursery firm Soupert et Notting in the mid-1870s and is remembered among collectors for its richly fragrant, deep velvety red blooms that age toward a dusky purplish maroon. The full, old-fashioned flowers open on a sturdy, moderately vigorous shrub with a strong spring bloom and lighter repeat later in the season. It thrives in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and benefits from moderate feeding during the growing season. Prune in late winter to remove old wood and maintain an open, productive framework.

common_name: Marbree Rose (Antique Mottled Pink Portland Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown own-root shrubs in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Marbree was raised by the French breeders Robert et Moreau and introduced in 1858, and takes its name from the distinctively mottled, marbled pattern of carmine-pink splashed over a lighter blush ground on each semi-double bloom. Like other Portland roses, it grows as a compact, upright shrub with fragrant flowers produced in a strong spring flush and useful repeat into fall. It performs well in smaller garden beds or mixed borders where its modest size is an asset, and prefers fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Prune lightly in late winter and deadhead through the season to encourage continued bloom.

common_name: Blanc de Vibert Rose (Antique White Portland Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown own-root shrubs in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Blanc de Vibert was raised by the French breeder Jean-Pierre Vibert, whom its name honors, and introduced around 1847, and remains valued as one of the few reliably white roses in the Portland class. Its fully double blooms open from blush-tinted buds to pure white and carry the strong, spicy damask fragrance typical of this group. The compact, upright shrub repeats well through the season, making it a useful fragrant white for beds and borders too small for larger antique roses. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and prune lightly in late winter to keep the shrub tidy and productive.
